subtopics.name: Acute kidney injury and chronic kidney disease

questions.stem: A 78-year-old client has had severe vomiting and diarrhea for 3 days. The blood pressure is 92/58 mm Hg, and the urine output is 15 mL/hr. The creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 1.8 mg/dL. Which finding suggests that the acute kidney injury is prerenal?

options.text: A BUN-to-creatinine ratio over 20:1 and concentrated urine
Muddy brown granular casts seen in the urine sediment
Hydronephrosis of both kidneys seen on the renal ultrasound
Red blood cell casts and heavy protein in the urine

rationale.correct: Prerenal AKI comes from poor perfusion (dehydration, hemorrhage, heart failure) and often reverses with fluids.

perOption.a: Low kidney perfusion leads to reabsorption of urea and water, giving a high BUN:creatinine ratio and concentrated urine.
perOption.b: These suggest acute tubular necrosis, an intrarenal cause.
perOption.c: This suggests a postrenal obstruction.
perOption.d: These suggest glomerulonephritis.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client in the oliguric phase of acute kidney injury after a cardiac arrest has a urine output of 200 mL in 24 hours, has gained 2 kg and has crackles at both lung bases. Which laboratory value is the nurse's priority to monitor?

options.text: Potassium
Hemoglobin
Albumin
Glucose

rationale.correct: During oliguria, watch potassium, fluid overload and acidosis.

perOption.a: The kidneys cannot excrete potassium, so hyperkalemia can cause fatal dysrhythmias.
perOption.b: Anemia develops more slowly.
perOption.c: Albumin is not the immediate risk.
perOption.d: Glucose is not the main risk.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client with stage 4 chronic kidney disease, a potassium of 5.6 mEq/L and a phosphorus of 6.2 mg/dL about diet. Which lunch choice shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: A turkey sandwich on white bread with apple slices
A baked potato with cheese and a glass of orange juice
White rice with green beans and a small chicken breast
A salad of lettuce and cucumber with an oil dressing

rationale.correct: CKD diets usually limit potassium, phosphorus, sodium and fluid, with moderate protein before dialysis.

perOption.a: These are lower in potassium and phosphorus.
perOption.b: Potatoes and orange juice are high in potassium, and cheese is high in phosphorus.
perOption.c: These are lower in potassium and phosphorus.
perOption.d: These are low in potassium and phosphorus.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing laboratory results for a client with stage 5 chronic kidney disease who is not yet on dialysis and reports fatigue and itching. Which findings should the nurse expect? Select all that apply.

options.text: Low hemoglobin
High phosphorus
Low calcium
High potassium
Low potassium
High bicarbonate

rationale.correct: End-stage CKD causes anemia, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, metabolic acidosis and fluid overload.

perOption.a: The kidneys make less erythropoietin.
perOption.b: Phosphorus builds up because the kidneys cannot excrete it.
perOption.c: Calcium falls as phosphorus rises and vitamin D activation drops.
perOption.d: Potassium builds up.
perOption.e: Potassium usually rises in end-stage kidney disease.
perOption.f: The kidneys cannot excrete acid, so bicarbonate falls (metabolic acidosis).

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize complications of chronic kidney disease.

questions.stem: A client with chronic kidney disease is due for epoetin alfa subcutaneously. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider before giving it?

options.text: A hemoglobin of 9.2 g/dL
A blood pressure of 182/104 mm Hg
A ferritin and iron level in the normal range
Mild fatigue after walking to the bathroom

rationale.correct: Before epoetin, check blood pressure and hemoglobin; the target is usually below about 11 g/dL to reduce cardiovascular risk.

perOption.a: Anemia is the reason for the drug.
perOption.b: Epoetin can raise blood pressure and increase stroke risk; uncontrolled hypertension is a reason to hold it.
perOption.c: Adequate iron is needed for epoetin to work.
perOption.d: Fatigue is a symptom of the anemia being treated.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Check safety parameters before giving epoetin.

questions.stem: A client with chronic kidney disease and a phosphorus of 6.4 mg/dL is starting sevelamer. The client asks when to take it. What should the nurse say?

options.text: "Take it at bedtime so it works overnight."
"Take it with each meal."
"Take it on an empty stomach before breakfast."
"Take it once a week on the same day."

rationale.correct: Phosphate binders such as sevelamer and calcium acetate are taken with meals.

perOption.a: It must be taken with food to bind dietary phosphorus.
perOption.b: Phosphate binders bind phosphorus in food so it is not absorbed.
perOption.c: Without food there is no phosphorus to bind.
perOption.d: It is taken with every meal.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach correct timing of phosphate binders.

questions.stem: A client has a new arteriovenous fistula in the left forearm for hemodialysis. The charge nurse is observing staff. Which action requires the charge nurse to intervene?

options.text: An LPN feels for a thrill over the fistula at the start of the shift
The RN listens for a bruit over the fistula with a stethoscope
An AP takes the blood pressure using the client's left arm
A phlebotomist draws the morning blood from the right arm

rationale.correct: Protect the access arm: no blood pressures, IVs or blood draws, and no tight clothing on that arm.

perOption.a: Feeling the thrill confirms flow.
perOption.b: Hearing the bruit confirms flow.
perOption.c: Compressing the fistula arm can damage the access or cause it to clot.
perOption.d: Using the other arm protects the access.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: During morning assessment of a client who receives hemodialysis three times a week, the nurse cannot feel a thrill or hear a bruit over the arteriovenous fistula. Yesterday both were present. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Document the finding as expected on a non-dialysis day
Notify the provider right away
Apply a warm compress and recheck it tomorrow
Flush the fistula gently with normal saline

rationale.correct: Loss of the thrill or bruit means thrombosis until proven otherwise.

perOption.a: An absent thrill and bruit is never normal.
perOption.b: This suggests the fistula has clotted, and early treatment may save it.
perOption.c: Delay risks losing the access.
perOption.d: Fistulas are not flushed.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with a BUN of 140 mg/dL is having a first hemodialysis session. Near the end of the session, the client reports a headache and nausea and becomes restless and confused. The blood pressure is 138/84. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome
Hyperkalemia from inadequate dialysis
Fluid overload from the dialysis circuit
Air embolism from the dialysis lines

rationale.correct: Disequilibrium syndrome is most likely in early sessions with a very high BUN; slower, shorter dialysis helps prevent it.

perOption.a: Rapid removal of urea causes fluid to shift into the brain, giving headache, nausea, restlessness and confusion.
perOption.b: Dialysis lowers potassium.
perOption.c: Dialysis removes fluid.
perOption.d: Air embolism causes sudden chest pain and dyspnea.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client on home peritoneal dialysis calls the clinic. The dialysate coming out has been cloudy since yesterday, and the client has abdominal pain and a temperature of 38.2 °C (100.8 °F). What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Peritonitis
Normal drainage
Constipation
Fluid overload

rationale.correct: Report cloudy effluent; a sample is sent for cell count and culture, and antibiotics are usually started.

perOption.a: Cloudy effluent with abdominal pain and fever is the classic sign of peritonitis.
perOption.b: Effluent should be clear and pale yellow.
perOption.c: Constipation slows outflow but does not make it cloudy.
perOption.d: This does not make the effluent cloudy.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: During an exchange, the outflow of a client's peritoneal dialysate is slow, and only half of the expected volume has drained. The client has not had a bowel movement in 3 days. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Turn the client side to side and check the tubing for kinks
Draw the fluid out of the catheter with a large syringe
Raise the drainage bag above the level of the abdomen
Call the provider to have the catheter removed

rationale.correct: Slow outflow is often due to position, kinks, a full bowel or catheter migration; check these first and treat constipation.

perOption.a: Repositioning and straightening the tubing often restore flow.
perOption.b: Forcing fluid can damage the catheter and the peritoneum.
perOption.c: The bag should be below the abdomen so gravity drains it.
perOption.d: This is premature; simple measures come first.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a 28-year-old woman who has had three urinary tract infections in a year. Which statement shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll wipe from front to back after using the toilet."
"I'll urinate soon after sexual intercourse."
"I'll take a bubble bath every day to keep clean."
"I'll drink plenty of water throughout the day."

rationale.correct: UTI prevention: fluids, frequent voiding, voiding after intercourse, front-to-back hygiene and avoiding irritants.

perOption.a: This reduces bacteria entering the urethra.
perOption.b: This flushes bacteria out.
perOption.c: Bubble baths can irritate the urethra; showers are preferred.
perOption.d: Fluids flush the bladder.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old client has burning on urination and urinary frequency. Which additional findings most suggest pyelonephritis rather than a bladder infection?

options.text: Burning that is worst at the very end of urination
Fever, chills and flank pain with CVA tenderness
Needing to urinate every 30 minutes
Cloudy urine with a strong odor

rationale.correct: Upper urinary tract infection causes systemic signs and flank pain with costovertebral angle tenderness.

perOption.a: This occurs with both.
perOption.b: These show the infection has reached the kidney.
perOption.c: This is common to both.
perOption.d: This is common to both.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client is admitted with severe right flank pain radiating to the groin from a suspected 4 mm kidney stone. Pain is controlled with IV ketorolac. Which instruction is most important for the nurse to give?

options.text: Strain all urine and save anything that is caught
Limit fluids to 1 L a day to reduce the pain
Stay in bed and rest until the stone has fully passed
Avoid all milk, cheese and yogurt

rationale.correct: Kidney stone care: pain control, fluids, walking and straining the urine to catch the stone.

perOption.a: Catching the stone allows analysis and guides prevention.
perOption.b: Fluids help pass the stone, unless restricted for another reason.
perOption.c: Walking may help the stone pass.
perOption.d: Calcium restriction is not routinely recommended.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Plan care for a client with a kidney stone.

questions.stem: A client with a kidney stone is pacing, crying and rating flank pain as 10 out of 10. The client also asks how to prevent future stones. What is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Pain management
Diet teaching
Intake and output
A 24-hour urine

rationale.correct: Renal colic is severe; treat the pain first, then teach.

perOption.a: Renal colic is extremely painful; analgesia, often NSAIDs and opioids, is the priority.
perOption.b: Teaching comes after the pain is controlled.
perOption.c: This matters but is not the priority.
perOption.d: This comes later.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize pain management in renal colic.

questions.stem: A client started phenazopyridine yesterday for UTI discomfort and calls the clinic saying, "My urine is bright orange." What should the nurse tell the client?

options.text: "This is an expected effect of the medicine."
"Stop the medicine right away and call back."
"This means there's blood in your urine."
"Go to the emergency department now."

rationale.correct: Phenazopyridine is a urinary analgesic that turns urine orange; it is used only short term.

perOption.a: Phenazopyridine turns urine red-orange and can stain clothing and contact lenses.
perOption.b: The color change is harmless.
perOption.c: The color comes from the drug.
perOption.d: This is not an emergency.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach the expected effects of phenazopyridine.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old client with benign prostatic hyperplasia is starting tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily. The client also takes lisinopril. Which instruction should the nurse give?

options.text: "Take it 30 minutes after the same meal each day and get up slowly."
"Take it only on the days when you have trouble starting your stream."
"Drink more coffee to help your bladder empty fully."
"It will shrink your prostate within a few days."

rationale.correct: Alpha blockers relax the prostate and bladder neck but can cause dizziness and orthostatic hypotension.

perOption.a: Tamsulosin can cause orthostatic hypotension, especially with early doses and with other blood pressure drugs.
perOption.b: It is taken every day.
perOption.c: Caffeine can worsen urgency.
perOption.d: Tamsulosin relaxes smooth muscle; it does not shrink the prostate.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client is receiving continuous bladder irrigation after a transurethral resection of the prostate. The drainage is bright red with clots, the output over the last hour is less than the irrigation inflow, and the client reports bladder spasms. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Increase the irrigation rate to clear the clots
Check the catheter for kinks or clots and irrigate per protocol
Clamp the catheter until the spasms settle
Give the PRN belladonna and opium suppository and reassess in an hour

rationale.correct: After TURP, keep the catheter draining; output should exceed the irrigant, and the irrigation rate is adjusted to keep the drainage light pink.

perOption.a: Increasing inflow while outflow is blocked distends the bladder.
perOption.b: Less output than input suggests obstruction, which must be cleared.
perOption.c: Clamping worsens retention and bleeding.
perOption.d: Treating spasms helps later, but the obstruction must be cleared first.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Manage continuous bladder irrigation after TURP.

questions.stem: A client receiving continuous bladder irrigation after a prostate resection has 3,200 mL of drainage in the collection bag at the end of an 8-hour shift. The irrigation solution used in the same period was 2,000 mL. What is the client's actual urine output for the shift?

rationale.correct: True urine output = total drainage − irrigation volume = 3,200 − 2,000 = 1,200 mL.
references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Calculate true urine output during bladder irrigation.

questions.stem: The nurse is rounding on clients with indwelling urinary catheters. Which observation requires the nurse to intervene to prevent a catheter-associated urinary tract infection?

options.text: A drainage bag hanging from the bed frame below the level of the bladder
A drainage bag hooked onto the rail at shoulder height for transport
A catheter secured to the upper thigh with a securement device
A closed system with the drainage port kept clamped and covered

rationale.correct: CAUTI prevention: remove catheters as soon as possible, keep the bag below the bladder and off the floor, and keep the system closed.

perOption.a: This prevents backflow.
perOption.b: Raising the bag above the bladder lets urine flow back into it.
perOption.c: This prevents movement and urethral irritation.
perOption.d: A closed system reduces infection.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: While inserting a urinary catheter in a female client, the nurse realizes the catheter has gone into the vagina. No urine returns. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Remove the catheter and reinsert it into the urethra right away
Leave it in place; insert a new sterile catheter in the urethra
Wipe the catheter with antiseptic, then reinsert it in the urethra
Stop the procedure and try again on the next shift

rationale.correct: A contaminated catheter is never reinserted; use a new sterile one.

perOption.a: The catheter is now contaminated.
perOption.b: The misplaced catheter marks where not to go, and a new sterile catheter prevents infection.
perOption.c: Wiping does not restore sterility.
perOption.d: The client still needs the catheter now.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: Eight hours after a spinal anesthetic for a knee replacement, a client has not urinated and reports lower abdominal fullness. The client has received 1,600 mL of IV fluid. The provider has prescribed intermittent catheterization for retention over 400 mL. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Insert an indwelling catheter to drain the bladder
Scan the bladder with a bladder scanner
Restrict oral and IV fluids until the client voids
Ask the provider for a dose of IV furosemide

rationale.correct: Assess first: palpate the bladder and use a bladder scan before catheterizing.

perOption.a: Retention should be confirmed first, and an intermittent catheter is prescribed.
perOption.b: A bladder scan measures retained urine and guides the next step.
perOption.c: This does not treat retention.
perOption.d: A diuretic would add to the bladder volume.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with type 2 diabetes and a creatinine of 1.6 mg/dL is scheduled for a CT scan with IV contrast. The client takes ibuprofen for arthritis. Which intervention best prevents contrast-induced kidney injury?

options.text: Restrict fluids for 12 hours before the scan to limit urine
Give IV or oral hydration before and after, as prescribed
Give a potassium supplement the morning of the scan
Take ibuprofen after the scan for any discomfort

rationale.correct: Prevent contrast nephropathy with hydration, holding nephrotoxic drugs such as NSAIDs and monitoring creatinine.

perOption.a: Dehydration increases the risk.
perOption.b: Hydration dilutes the contrast and keeps urine flowing.
perOption.c: This does not protect the kidneys.
perOption.d: NSAIDs increase the risk of kidney injury.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: Two weeks after a strep throat infection, a 9-year-old has tea-colored urine, puffiness around the eyes that is worse in the morning, a decreased urine output and a blood pressure of 138/92 mm Hg. The urinalysis shows red cells and red cell casts. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
A lower urinary tract infection
A kidney stone in the ureter
Nephrotic syndrome after the infection

rationale.correct: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis: cola-colored urine, edema and hypertension 1 to 3 weeks after a strep infection.

perOption.a: Hematuria, edema and hypertension after a strep infection are typical.
perOption.b: A UTI does not cause periorbital edema and hypertension.
perOption.c: Stones cause pain, not edema and hypertension.
perOption.d: Nephrotic syndrome causes heavy proteinuria and edema, usually without hypertension and cola-colored urine.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old client with long-standing diabetes and hypertension has routine kidney function tests at a clinic visit. For each result, select the interpretation.

options.text: Low
Within normal range
High
Low
Within normal range
High
Low
Within normal range
High

rationale.correct: A raised BUN and creatinine with a low GFR show reduced kidney function.

perOption.b1:a: The result is high, not low.
perOption.b1:b: The result is high, not within normal range.
perOption.b1:c: Normal BUN is about 10 to 20 mg/dL.
perOption.b2:a: The result is high, not low.
perOption.b2:b: The result is high, not within normal range.
perOption.b2:c: Normal creatinine is about 0.6 to 1.2 mg/dL.
perOption.b3:a: A GFR below 60 for 3 months or more indicates CKD; 15 to 29 is stage 4.
perOption.b3:b: The result is low, not within normal range.
perOption.b3:c: The result is low, not high.

references: Laboratory reference ranges as used in common NCLEX review texts; follow the facility's ranges
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: Three months after a kidney transplant, a client who takes tacrolimus, mycophenolate and prednisone calls the clinic. Which report should the nurse act on right away?

options.text: Fever, tenderness over the transplant and less urine
A bigger appetite and some weight gain over the month
A mild hand tremor, mostly noticed when writing
Weight unchanged and urine output the same as last week

rationale.correct: Signs of rejection: fever, graft tenderness, falling urine output, weight gain and a rising creatinine.

perOption.a: These may signal rejection or infection, both of which need prompt treatment.
perOption.b: This is often due to steroids.
perOption.c: This is a common side effect of tacrolimus; it is reported but is not urgent.
perOption.d: This is reassuring.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize signs of kidney transplant rejection.
